module_title: Banking and Financial Awareness: History and Types of Banks in India (Level 3)
introduction: At this advanced level, we analyze the complexities of the banking structure, the Banking Regulation Act (1949), All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs), D-SIBs (Too Big To Fail), and the Mega Mergers of PSBs. This is crucial for RBI Grade B, IBPS PO Mains, and SBI PO Mains.

core_concepts.title: Banking Regulation Act, 1949
core_concepts.description:
All banks in India are governed by this act. Important sections tested in Mains:
- Section 22: Licensing of banks.
- Section 24: Maintenance of Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR).
- Section 35A: Power of the RBI to give directions to banks in public interest (used recently to restrict Paytm Payments Bank).

core_concepts.title: D-SIBs (Domestic Systemically Important Banks)
core_concepts.description: These are banks classified as 'Too Big To Fail'. Their collapse would severely disrupt the broader economy. The RBI currently classifies only three banks as D-SIBs: SBI, ICICI Bank, and HDFC Bank. They are required to maintain additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital.

core_concepts.title: All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)
core_concepts.description:
These are apex developmental banks regulated directly by the RBI to boost specific sectors:
1. NABARD (Agriculture and Rural Development)
2. SIDBI (MSMEs - Headquartered in Lucknow)
3. EXIM Bank (Export and Import)
4. NHB (Housing Finance)
5. NaBFID (National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development - the 5th and newest AIFI).

core_concepts.title: Mega Merger of Public Sector Banks
core_concepts.description:
In 2019-2020, the government merged 10 large PSBs into 4 to create global-sized strong banks. 
Key mergers: Oriental Bank of Commerce (OBC) and United Bank of India merged into PNB; Syndicate Bank merged into Canara Bank; Allahabad Bank merged into Indian Bank; Andhra Bank and Corporation Bank merged into Union Bank of India.

important_entities.name: DICGC (Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation)
important_entities.key_fact: Provides deposit insurance to bank customers if a bank fails.
important_entities.significance: A wholly-owned subsidiary of the RBI, it ensures each depositor up to a maximum of ₹5,00,000 (inclusive of principal and interest). It covers all commercial, regional rural, and cooperative banks.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Banks vs. NBFCs (Non-Banking Financial Companies) Mega Trap
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation:
A favorite for Mains exams. Key differences:
1. NBFCs CANNOT accept demand deposits (Current & Savings Accounts - CASA).
2. NBFCs do not form part of the payment and settlement system and cannot issue self-drawn cheques.
3. The deposit insurance facility of DICGC is NOT available to depositors of NBFCs.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: PNB = OBC + United Bank (O-U). Canara Bank = Syndicate Bank. In Mains, you will often face 'Match the Following' questions pairing the Anchor Bank with the Amalgamating Bank.

exam_strategy_tips: For RBI Grade B, strictly link these concepts with Basel III norms, Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB), and exact Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) percentages (e.g., 9% + 2.5% = 11.5%).
Keep track of the authorized capital of newly formed institutions. For example, NaBFID was established with an authorized share capital of ₹1 lakh crore and initial paid-up capital of ₹20,000 crore.
